analytic.title: Response Time Analysis for Real-Time DAG Tasks Under Partitioned Scheduling

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Parallel task systems with real-time constraints are widely applied in various fields. Response time analysis is a necessary condition for online admission of applications in dynamic systems. This article focuses on the worst-case response time (WCRT) analysis of directed acyclic graph (DAG) tasks on multiprocessors under partitioned scheduling. We propose a new WCRT analysis algorithm, named the radiative-extended structure analysis (RESA) algorithm. We demonstrate that analyzing the radiative-extended structure (Res) helps to obtain more accurate analysis results. Compared with state-of-theart algorithms, RESA achieves tighter upper bounds on selfinterference and high-priority interference without increasing time and space complexity. RESA performs better by comparing the average response time observed in simulation experiments. Index Terms-Real-time multiprocessor system, partitioned scheduling, directed acyclic graph, worst-case response time.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: T ASK scheduling is a critical issue in the field of mul- tiprocessor systems [1][2][3][4]. In real-time scheduling problems, given a limited number of tasks, each task sequentially releases an infinite number of jobs. The scheduling algorithm schedules tasks in real-time and allocates computing resources to complete all tasks within time constraints and avoid scheduling failures [5]. The performance of schedulability analysis is crucial for real-time multiprocessor systems [5][6][7]. In dynamic systems, requests for new real-time tasks may arrive during execution time [8]. Before such tasks (such as multimedia applications) can be allowed to enter the system, schedulability analysis must be performed [6]. Therefore, in this case, it is necessary to perform schedulability analysis as quickly as possible to allow for rapid response to request for new realtime jobs [8][9][10]. The central aspect of schedulability analysis is to evaluate the worst-case response time (WCRT). WCRT analysis is used for predicting real-time system behavior. Excellent WCRT analysis algorithms can not only predict the operational behavior of multiprocessor systems but also serve as a reference indicator for whether to add new tasks to the system [11][12][13]. As multiprocessor platforms become mainstream, accurate analysis of WCRT is crucial for improving system utilization and performance evaluation accuracy [11][12][13]. Compared to single processor, WCRT analysis of realtime task scheduling algorithms on multiple processors is usually much more complex [8][9][10].

Real-time tasks on multiprocessors are often modeled as directed acyclic graphs (DAG) [14]. In this model, DAG task consists of several subtasks with topological constraints [14]. The topological constraints between different subtasks significantly affect the execution of DAG tasks, so accurately analyzing the WCRT of DAG tasks is a challenge. This article analyzes the execution behavior of specific parallel structures widely present in DAG tasks and calculates the WCRT under partitioned scheduling with fixed priority. Specifically, we defined a specific parallel structure called the radiative-extended structure (Res) and analyzed its execution behavior in multiprocessor system. We proved that Res's execution behavior analysis helping achieve stricter upper bounds on self-interference and high-priority interference in WCRT analysis method. Finally, based on the execution behavior analysis of Res, we propose a new WCRT analysis algorithm, called the radiative-extended structure analysis (RESA) algorithm, which achieves stricter analysis results than existing state-of-the-art algorithm.
The main contributions of this paper are as follows:

• We defined a specific parallel structure called Res and analyzed the execution behavior of the Res in DAG tasks. We demonstrated and proved that analyzing Res's execution behavior may significantly improve the accuracy of self-interference and high-priority interference analysis. Compared with similar algorithms, we are the first research to reduce the upper bound of self-interference and further reduce the upper bound of high-priority interference.
• We proposed the WCRT analysis algorithm (RESA) and validated its performance through simulation experiments.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In section II, we introduce the real-time task model in this research. In section III, we introduce two existing partitioned scheduling WCRT analysis algorithms for subsequent performance comparison. In section IV, we present new upper bounds for self-interference and high-priority interference and a new WCRT analysis algorithm (RESA). Section V describes simulation experiment results. Section VII summarizes this article and proposes our future research direction.

div.head: II. SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: We consider a familiar system model in real-time scheduling problems [15]. What needs to be scheduled on a homogeneous multiprocessor platform is a set Γ of N directed acyclic graph (DAG) tasks. The multiprocessor platform has m homogeneous processors composed of p 1 , • • • , p m . Each DAG task is expressed as τ i = (V i , E i , T i , D i , π i ) where V i denotes the set of subtasks, E i the set of directed edges, T i the arrival period, D i the relative deadline and π i the fixed unique priority. In this paper, we make a reasonable simplification D i = T i [15]. A DAG task τ j has higher priority than τ i only if j < i. A set hp(τ i ) represents the DAG tasks with higher priority than τ i .

Then, we introduce the specific DAG task model. v i,j ∈ V i represents the j th subtask of task τ i . For each subtask v i,j , P i,j is the allocated processor and there is a relative execution time parameter C i,j representing the worst-case execution time (WCET) on P i,j . Since the processors are homogeneous, each subtask has the same WCET across different processors. C i represents the WCET of τ i . To describe the duty cycle of a DAG task, the utilization of τ i is defined as U i and calculated by C i /T i . The whole task set Γ's utilization U is calculated by ∀τi∈Γ U i . The directed edge e(v i,s , v i,t ) from subtask v i,s to v i,t denotes their topology constraints where v i,s is the father subtask of v i,t and v i,t is the child subtask of v i,s . A child subtask can only begin executing until all father subtasks have been executed. A subtask with no father subtask is called an entry subtask, v entry . If a DAG has multiple entry subtasks, a dummy entry subtask with zero execution time and directed edges can be added to the graph. A subtask with no child subtask is called an exit subtask, v exit . Similar to the entry subtask, if a DAG has multiple exit subtasks, a dummy exit subtask with zero execution time and directed edges from the current multiple exit subtasks to this dummy subtask can be added to the graph [14]. During execution, each DAG task may release a infinite sequence of jobs. Once priorities are assigned to all DAG tasks in Γ, the priority is fixed and will not change during execution. Due to the characteristics of RTOS, when a higher priority subtask can be executed, it will preempt lower priority subtasks. At the same instant, τ i 's subtasks are released and subtasks cannot preempt each other because subtasks within the same task have an equivalent priority [15]. We assume all DAG tasks are allocated under partitioned scheduling with fixed priority, and each DAG task's priority and subtask's processors for executing have been allocated [15]. Fig. 1 is a DAG task τ i with C i = 95 and T i = D i = 100. V i,1 is an entry subtask. V i,3 , V i,7 and V i,8 are exit subtasks. div.head: III. WCRT ANALYSIS
div.p: In this section, we introduce a traditional WCRT analysis strategy, "response time algorithm" (RTA) [16], and the state-of-the-art WCRT analysis strategy at present, "reducing repetitive calculation" (RRC) [15] for preemptive fixed priority partitioned scheduling of DAG tasks.

div.head: A. RTA Analysis Strategy
div.p: Next, we will introduce a WCRT analysis algorithm proposed by Fonseca et al [16]. For DAG task τ i , the WCRT is equivalent to the longest WCRT among all paths and can be calculated by Equation1 [16]:

div.p: As shown in Equation1, R(λ i,k ) represents path λ i,k 's WCRT. It can be calculated by Equation2 [16]:

The third part I i (λ i,k ) is self-interference, which is caused by subtasks same in τ i but not in λ i,k .

div.head: B. RRC Analysis Strategy
div.p: Based on the WCRT analysis algorithm (RTA) mentioned above, the RRC analysis strategy reduced the high-priority interference I ub high (λ i,k ) by considering the potential parallelism in high-priority interference.

The RRC analysis strategy defines a parallel structure Str. Str i,r denotes the r th Str structure of task τ i [15]. All subtasks in Str i,r will be executed on processor set StrP i,r . W p i,r represents Str i,r 's total workload on processor p ∈ StrP i,r . The potential parallelism in the Str can further reduce the highpriority interference it generates. Subsequently, the RRC analysis strategy defines StrP j,r (λ i,k ) which representing union of pr(λ i,k ) and StrP j,r . All subtasks in Str j,r owned minimum parallel execution time among processor set StrP j,r (λ i,k ) is shown in Equation9 [15]:

div.p: IV. RESA

div.head: A. Radiative-Extend Structure
div.p: Radiative-extend structure (Res) represents a subset of a DAG with three layers. In the first layer, there is a subtask with two or more child subtasks, each with a unique father subtask. If the child subtasks in the second layer have only one second-level child subtask with a unique father subtask, this second-level child subtask forms the third layer of Res. Res i,j represents the j th radiative-extend structure in τ i .

We define this father subtask as Res i,j,0 , these child subtasks as Res i,j,1 , these second-level child subtasks as Res i,j,2 . Note that there may not be a subtask in Res i,j,2 . Fig. 2 illustrates a set Γ of 3 real-time DAG tasks. DAG1 has Res
The Res in a DAG task only depends on its topological relationships in adjacency matrix of τ i .

div.head: B. Res for Self-Interference
div.p: Among many WCRT analysis methods, self-interference as a pessimistic upper bound has yet to be optimized. In this section, we demonstrate an execution behavior of the Res and its role in reducing the upper bound of self-interference. Definition 2. For the child subtasks and second-level child subtasks in the Res, when one second-level child subtask V i,j is allocated to the same processor with child subtasks V s,t (not V i,j 's father subtask V m,n ), this will bring self-interference. However, the parallelism between subtasks V s,t and V m,n (they are not executed on a same processor) can reduce selfinterference. We call (V s,t , V i,j ) as ResP air.

In other words, if the path λ i,k has a subtask as V i,j in ResP air, the reduction of self-interference for this Res is G i . High-priority interference will not affect this conclusion. All Ress, which come from τ i , can be analyzed independently for self-interference, that is to say the analysis of each Res is not interfered by any other Ress in τ i . Because subtasks have direct topological relationships in the path λ i,k . The necessary condition for self-interference to occur is that there is no direct topological relationship. Therefore, if V i,j in ResP air appears in λ i,k , then there will be no V s,t appearing and one ResP air can only appear once in λ i,k .

The ResP air depends on processor partition in a Res. For a path λ i,k , we get ResP air i and self (λ i,k ) and find the union G(λ i,k ) of subtasks in both the path and the last subtask of ResP air i . Each subtask v i,x in this union will reduce selfinterference at least G i,x . The upper bound of self-interference can be rewritten as Equation12:

div.head: A. DAG Task Set Generation
div.p: To generalize the experimental results, we strive to maintain consistency with previous studies regarding DAG parameters and DAG generation tools. We control the generation of DAG task sets by the following four DAG parameters:
• U : the total utilization of Γ.
• m: the number of processors in multiprocessor system.
• N : the number of DAG tasks in Γ.

• p: the probability of creating edges. Hence, the total utilization of a task set Γ will be set from 1 to 2.4 with each step increment of 0.2. The Randfixedsum algorithm proposed by Emberson et al. will be used to generate each DAG task's utilization U i . The number of processors will be set from 4 to 32 with each step increment 2. The number of DAG tasks in a task set will be set from 10 to 30 with each step increment 2. The topological matrix of DAG task is generated by a DAG generation tool with G(|V i |, p) [17], and p will be set from 10 to 60 with each step increment 5. Each subtask has a WCET random from 1 to 100. After the above parameters are generated, T i can be calculated by C i /U i .

We use one DAG parameter as a variable each time and fix the remaining DAG parameters and test with four DAG parameters sequentially as variables to verify our WCRT analysis algorithm performance in various scenarios. The For processor partition strategies (random and EST), EST has better performance. Regardless of the processor allocation strategy's quality, the RESA algorithm demonstrates better performance. Similarly, in Fig. 5,6, we show the simulation results with varied utilization U i , and probability of creating edges p. In various scenarios, the RESA algorithm achieves more accurate WCRT analysis results, a higher acceptance ratio.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSIONS AND FUTUREWORK
div.p: This article defines a parallel structure Res under the DAG task model. By analyzing the execution behavior of the Res, we demonstrate that it can significantly reduce the upper bounds of self-interference and high-priority interference. Furthermore, we propose a new WCRT analysis algorithm, the RESA algorithm. Through theoretical analysis, simulation experiments, RESA performs better in WCRT analysis and acceptance ratio. Compared with the state-of-the-art algorithm, RESA achieved better WCRT analysis results.

We plan to address the following two issues in our future research. The first is how to apply this algorithm to more complex real-time heterogeneous multiprocessor systems. As artificial intelligence applications become more prevalent, heterogeneous multiprocessor systems are expected to see wider deployment. There is still very little research in this area. The second is to propose a new partitioned scheduling algorithm for real-time multiprocessor systems. Self-interference analysis and processor utilization can serve as heuristic indicators for partitioned scheduling. We can utilize self-interference analysis to predict the parallelism of DAG task sets and provide a more balanced processor allocation strategy.

Taking the number of processors as example, we generate one thousand DAG task sets at each number of processors for analyzing their average performances. We define the acceptance ratio as the percentage of schedulable task sets under a given value of m [15]. For instance, the acceptance ratio of 13 percent under m = 12 represents 130 task sets are schedulable. For average WCRT and acceptance ratio, we only count data from schedulable task sets.

div.head: B. Processor Allocation Strategies and Single Processor Scheduling Algorithm
div.p: We used two processor allocation strategies to test the impact of them:

To discuss the impact of processor allocation strategies, these two processor allocation strategies are tested on the same DAG task set. The first scenario of random processor allocation strategy aims to demonstrate the accuracy of the RESA algorithm, as well as the RTA algorithm and RRC algorithm, in general.

In real-time operating system, there are two common priority assignment algorithms, monotonic rate (RM) scheduling algorithm and deadline monotonous (DM) scheduling algorithm. We choose the DM scheduling algorithm as the single processor scheduling algorithm.

div.head: C. Experiment Results
div.p: In Fig. 3, we show the simulation data with varied number of processors (m from 4 to 32 with each step increment 2) when U = 2.4, N = 20, V = 20, p = 10. "RESrandom," "RRC-random," and "RTA-random" represent the DAG tasks analyzed by the RESA, RRC, and RTA algorithms under random processor allocation strategy, respectively. Similarly, "RES-EST," "RRC-EST," and "RTA-EST" represent the RESA, RRC, and RTA algorithms under the EST processor allocation strategy. In Fig. 3a, the average WCRT decreases with an increase in the number of processors. A WCRT analysis algorithm may not have experiment results at some lower number of processors because no task sets are schedulable in this situation. The RESA algorithm has a significantly shorter average WCRT than the RTA and RRC algorithms under the same processor allocation strategy. Fig. 3b shows the acceptance ratio with a varied number of processors based on the RESA, RRC, and RTA algorithms. The acceptance ratio increases when the number of processors increases. The acceptance ratios become zero when there is a lower number of processors. The RESA algorithm has a significantly higher acceptance ratio than the RTA and RRC when the processor number is same.

In Fig. 4, we show the simulation results with varied task number in a task set (N from 10 to 30 with each step increment 2) when m = 8, U = 1.4, V = 20, p = 10. The RESA algorithm obtains a significantly shorter average WCRT and significantly higher acceptance ratio in the same scenario.
